title: Untangling amino acid metabolism in renal diseases: mechanisms, dysregulation, and critical gaps

sections.abstract: Amino acid metabolism is closely linked with kidney physiology and pathology. In acute kidney injury, chronic kidney disease, diabetic kidney disease, and autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, disturbances in the branched-chain amino acids, tryptophan, glutamine, taurine, and sulfur amino acids pathways are consistently observed. Specific metabolites such as D-serine, kynurenine intermediates, and branched-chain keto acids are associated with disease progression. Taurine and indoxyl sulfate have also been proposed as therapeutic targets. At the nephron level, transporters and enzymes controlling amino acid flux influence nitrogen balance, oxidative stress, fibrosis, inflammation, and tubular injury. In chronic kidney disease, impaired amino acid handling contributes to protein-energy wasting, altered muscle metabolism, and systemic complications. In autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, cyst fluid metabolomics has revealed alterations in tryptophan and polyamine metabolism. The use of nutritional interventions, microbiome modulation, and selective supplementation as therapeutic strategies is being explored, although clinical trial evidence remains limited. Several key issues remain unresolved, including the need for isotope tracer studies to define renal amino acid kinetics in humans, the rigorous validation of metabolite biomarkers across diverse populations, the integration of diet and microbiome-derived metabolites into mechanistic frameworks, and the systematic evaluation of sex-specific differences. Longitudinal studies are scarce, thus restricting predictive power and therapeutic translation. Further mechanistic clarification may support the development of biomarkers and targeted therapies.
sections.introduction:
The kidney plays a central role in maintaining systemic amino acid homeostasis. Beyond filtration and excretion, the kidney governs reabsorption, transamination, gluconeogenesis, and nitrogen exchange, particularly within the proximal tubule, which is specialized for these processes [ 1 ]. Nearly all filtered amino acids are reclaimed under normal conditions, and the kidney makes critical contributions to acid–base balance through glutamine metabolism [ 2 , 3 ]. This metabolic activity sustains energy balance, protects against acidosis, and supports the structural integrity of the nephron.

Disruptions in the aforementioned pathways have been linked to major kidney disorders. Branched-chain amino acid (BCAA) catabolism is impaired in diabetic kidney disease (DKD), leading to metabolic stress, mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) activation, and mitochondrial dysfunction [ 4 , 5 ]. In autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD), methionine-driven nutrient sensing accelerates cyst growth by activating mTORC1 [ 6 ]. Tryptophan degradation via the kynurenine pathway contributes to inflammation and endothelial dysfunction, whereas microbial tryptophan metabolites such as indoxyl sulfate promote fibrosis and vascular injury [ 7 ]. Taurine, a conditionally essential amino sulfonic acid, has antioxidant and osmoregulatory roles, and it has potential benefits in diabetic and chronic kidney injury, although clinical data remain limited [ 8 , 9 ].

Altered amino acid metabolism is not only a secondary effect of renal impairment but also often contributes directly to injury and repair. In acute kidney injury (AKI), changes in polyamine turnover and amino acid flux influence regeneration and fibrosis [ 10 , 11 ]. In chronic kidney disease (CKD), dysregulated amino acid handling affects both glomerular and tubular compartments, thereby accelerating disease progression [ 12 ]. These findings demonstrate that metabolic shifts can have both protective effects and pathogenic effects.

This review aims to integrate mechanistic, clinical, and translational perspectives on amino acid metabolism in kidney disease, identify unresolved questions, and outline priorities for future research. Despite rapid advances in metabolomics and single-cell profiling, several gaps remain. Data concerning sex differences in amino acid handling, the impact of diet, and the role of the microbiome are incomplete [ 13 , 14 ]. Clinical in vivo flux studies are lacking. This limitation hampers the translation of data from experimental models [ 15 ]. Biomarkers such as D-serine and kynurenine are promising but require validation across diverse populations [ 16 , 17 ]. Owing to the limited length of this review, more details concerning topics covered by the following sections are provided in the Supplementary Appendix .
sections.conclusion:
Amino acid metabolism has essential links between renal physiology, systemic homeostasis, and disease progression. Several priorities for translation into clinical practice have been identified.

There is a need for better integration of mechanistic and clinical data. Clinical tracer studies remain scarce, but identifying which pathways drive clinical outcomes is essential. Future work should combine isotopic flux analysis with high-resolution metabolomics and transcriptomic or proteomic profiling to capture the dynamic regulation of renal amino acid handling in vivo . Standardized protocols for sample collection and isotope administration would improve comparability across studies.

Biomarkers derived from amino acid metabolism, including D-serine, kynurenine, and BCAAs, require validation in large, multicenter, and multiethnic populations. Analytical harmonization, interlaboratory calibration, and rigorous external replication are necessary for clinical translation. Cohorts incorporating dietary assessment, microbiome profiling, and longitudinal follow-up can help distinguish biological variability from true disease-related signals.

Therapeutic interventions based on amino acid metabolism should progress beyond feasibility studies. Very-low-protein diets supplemented with ketoacid analogs, taurine supplementation, and microbiome-directed strategies warrant adequately powered randomized trials with hard renal endpoints. The incorporation of metabolic phenotyping and biomarker-based stratification could improve trial efficiency and clarify which patient subgroups derive the greatest benefit.

Heterogeneity in patient populations must be addressed. Sex, diet, and microbiome composition influence amino acid metabolism and may explain inconsistencies across studies. The integration of these variables into biomarker discovery and interventional design is essential for precision-oriented approaches. In conclusion, amino acid metabolism is integral to kidney physiology and disease. Disturbances in the glutamine, BCAAs, tryptophan, and taurine pathways contribute to acidosis, sarcopenia, inflammation, and fibrosis. These processes generate both biomarkers and therapeutic targets. Future progress depends on coordinated mechanistic and translational studies that link metabolic alterations to clinical outcomes. If these challenges are met, amino acid biology could become an integral part of precision nephrology, thus facilitating earlier diagnosis and more individualized therapy.
